name: Non-Functional Requirement
subject: blockchain

lesson.title: The Requirements Nobody Demos: Writing Down What 'Good Enough' Means
lesson.summary: A non-functional requirement states, in specific and testable terms, how well a system must perform a function rather than what the function is, and it is the document that turns an abstract quality attribute into an obligation an architecture can be checked against.
lesson.body:
A functional requirement describes a feature: the contract shall allow a token holder to transfer tokens to another address. A non-functional requirement describes a constraint on how that feature has to behave: the transfer shall be confirmed within ten seconds at the 95th percentile under a load of five thousand transactions per second. Both sentences are requirements, and both belong in the same document, but only one of them can be checked off by clicking through a demo. The other has to be measured, often under conditions that do not show up until the system is already under real stress.

The relationship to quality attribute is close enough that people sometimes use the two terms interchangeably, but the distinction is worth keeping. Quality attribute names the category, performance, security, modifiability, and so on, in the abstract, the way it was introduced earlier in this chapter. A non-functional requirement is what happens when a team takes that abstract category and pins it to a specific, falsifiable number for a specific project. Performance as a quality attribute is a concern. Confirm 95 percent of transactions within ten seconds under five thousand transactions per second of load is a non-functional requirement, something an engineer can actually test against and either pass or fail.

Those specific numbers should trace back to an actual business need, which is where stakeholder analysis and business requirements do their work. A bank settling large interbank transfers can tolerate a finality time of minutes, because the value of certainty outweighs the value of speed for a transaction of that size. A mobile game issuing small in-app rewards needs confirmation closer to instant, because a player who has to wait thirty seconds to see an item appear will assume the app is broken. The quality attribute in both cases is the same, finality time, but the non-functional requirement that follows from it is completely different, because it is derived from what each business actually needs rather than from a generic notion of good performance.

Bitcoin's roughly ten minute block target is itself a non-functional requirement baked directly into consensus, chosen deliberately to give the network time to propagate blocks globally and limit orphan rates, at the cost of a settlement time that is far too slow for point of sale retail purchases. That mismatch between the base layer's non-functional requirement and what merchants actually need is exactly why systems like the Lightning Network exist, layered on top specifically to satisfy a finality and cost requirement the base chain was never designed to meet without redesigning its consensus mechanism from scratch.

The failure mode worth watching for is a project that writes exhaustive functional specifications, page after page describing exactly what a smart contract does, while leaving every non-functional requirement implicit or unstated. That gap rarely shows up during development, when everything is tested at small scale by a friendly internal team. It shows up months later, during a traffic spike, a targeted attack, or the first time someone tries to audit the system's behavior against a regulation nobody wrote down as a requirement in the first place. Writing non-functional requirements down before choosing an architecture, not after building one, is what turns "good enough" from a hope into something the team can actually verify.
